claims.claim: The first 60-watt-equivalent LED replacement bulbs, released around 2010 by Sylvania and Philips, cost about $40 per bulb.
claims.episode_span: In 2010 a typical LED replacement for a 60-watt incandescent carried a retail price between forty and fifty dollars.
claims.source_title: How LED Lights Became So Cheap - distilled.earth
claims.supporting_quote: By 2010 Sylvania and Philips released their first 60-watt-equivalent LED bulb (the type of light bulb you’d want to put in a lamp). It cost $40 per bulb.

claims.claim: An equivalent LED bulb today sells for a few dollars or less (under $2).
claims.episode_span: The same light output today is available for two to three dollars.
claims.source_title: How LED Lights Became So Cheap - distilled.earth
claims.supporting_quote: Today, you can buy an LED light bulb for less than $2.

claims.claim: LED bulb costs fell roughly 90% between 2008 and the mid-2010s, with early single bulbs costing as much as $100.
claims.episode_span: Retail prices fell more than 90 percent while efficacy roughly doubled.
claims.source_title: Saving American Families and Businesses Money through Lighting Efficiency | Department of Energy
claims.supporting_quote: total installations of common home LED bulbs increased six-fold from 13 million to 78 million – growth enabled by the nearly 90% reduction in cost since 2008.

claims.claim: The yellow phosphor in white LEDs is cerium-doped yttrium aluminium garnet (Ce:YAG).
claims.episode_span: The phosphor layer that converts blue emission to broad-spectrum white uses a few milligrams of yttrium-aluminum-garnet doped with cerium
claims.supporting_quote: A common yellow phosphor material is cerium - doped yttrium aluminium garnet

claims.claim: White-LED gallium-nitride dies are conventionally grown on sapphire substrates (with silicon carbide and silicon as alternatives).
claims.episode_span: a few square millimeters of gallium-nitride material grown on sapphire or silicon carbide.
claims.supporting_quote: (GaN-on-Si) is being used to produce white LEDs using 200-mm silicon wafers. This avoids the typical costly sapphire substrate

claims.claim: LED lamp efficacy passed through the ~80-100+ lumens-per-watt range in the mid-2010s (about 83 lm/W in 2014, projected above 150 lm/W by 2020).
claims.episode_span: As efficacy rose from roughly 60 lumens per watt to more than 100, the waste heat per lumen fell sharply.
claims.source_title: LED bulb efficiency expected to continue improving as cost declines - U.S. Energy Information Administration
claims.supporting_quote: Solid-state light-emitting diode (LED) lamps are even more efficient—currently producing around 83 lumens per Watt
